1. Executive Summary
FlowStore is feasible as a bounded, local system-design virtual lab for demonstrating a time-series storage
and ingestion pipeline. The known implementation combines a configurable record generator, bounded
queue, validation/processing stage, partition buffers, chunk builder, Parquet writer, SQLite metadata, and
persistent local files. A React and TypeScript interface uses React Flow to visualize the pipeline, while a
Python FastAPI backend and WebSockets support control and live telemetry.
The prototype can demonstrate the relationship between offered load, actual throughput, queue depth,
buffering, chunk formation, and persistence, provided each displayed metric is derived from the running
engine. It can also support controlled comparisons across workload presets. This report does not claim
production scalability or measured performance values that have not been supplied; those must be recorded
from actual runs.

2. Problem and Objectives
Time-series applications produce timestamped measurements such as CPU usage, memory usage, request
rates, device telemetry, and disk activity. These records may arrive continuously or in bursts. If the
ingestion pipeline cannot process or persist records as quickly as they arrive, queues and buffers can grow,
latency can rise, and data may be delayed or rejected depending on the system's policy.
FlowStore addresses the design problem by separating ingestion into observable stages instead of treating
storage as one opaque operation. Its virtual-lab interface is intended to help students vary workload
parameters, observe how each stage behaves, and identify potential bottlenecks.
Objectives: (1) generate a configurable number of time-series records; (2) distinguish target feed rate from
measured throughput; (3) use a bounded queue and expose queue pressure; (4) validate records and track
accepted/rejected counts; (5) partition and buffer accepted records; (6) build chunks and persist them as
Parquet; (7) maintain local run/file metadata; and (8) compare controlled experiments using truthful
telemetry.

3. Scope and Assumptions
3.1 In scope. The local prototype includes a configurable generator, bounded queue, processor, partition
buffers, chunk builder, Parquet persistence, SQLite metadata, a web interface, live updates, event logs, run
history, and storage exploration to the extent supported by the current repository.
3.2 Out of scope. The known design is a local prototype and does not by itself establish distributed
ingestion, multi-node coordination, replicated metadata, cloud durability, multi-tenant security, or
production-scale capacity. Cloud integration is a possible extension, not an assumed current feature.
3.3 Assumptions. Runs execute on a single development environment unless the implementation proves
otherwise. Metrics depend on the host machine, configured workload, and measurement interval. Any exact
flush conditions, queue overflow behavior, recovery guarantees, and latency percentiles must match the
actual code and should not be assumed if they are not implemented.

4. System Overview
FlowStore accepts configuration such as target record count, target feed rate, chunk size, writer delay, and
invalid-record ratio. The generator creates records and sends them to a bounded queue. The processor
validates each record, updates accepted/rejected counters, and routes accepted records to partition buffers.
The chunk builder groups records into chunks, and the Parquet writer persists completed chunks. SQLite
metadata and local storage support run history and file inspection.
The browser interface visualizes the pipeline and its metrics. FastAPI exposes the control and information
endpoints, while WebSockets can deliver live events and metric updates. The visualization is an
observability layer: the engine remains the source of truth for processing and persistence outcomes.

5. Technical Feasibility
The core technologies are established and suitable for a local academic prototype. React Flow can represent
the pipeline topology, FastAPI can provide HTTP and WebSocket interfaces, PyArrow can write Parquet
files, and SQLite can maintain local metadata. Docker Compose can provide a repeatable local environment
with persistent data mounted outside the container's ephemeral filesystem.
Technical feasibility depends on keeping metric definitions consistent and validating the lifecycle of a run.
The displayed generated, accepted, rejected, buffered, chunked, and persisted counts should reconcile
according to the engine's exact semantics. A stopped run should terminate its background tasks; a
completed run should retain its final metrics; and a successful persistence count should only increase after
the writer confirms success.

6. Operational Feasibility
FlowStore is operationally feasible for a local demonstration when the frontend, API, engine, and persistent
data directories can be started repeatably. Docker Compose reduces environment setup friction. Run history
and the storage explorer help users inspect prior runs and confirm that generated outputs remain available.
Operational validation should include starting a run, observing live updates, stopping a run before
completion, completing a full run, restarting the services, and verifying that previously persisted files and
metadata remain available. This report does not assert that every scenario has passed; the final submission
should include test evidence from the actual implementation.

7. Storage Benefit and Performance Feasibility
FlowStore is not a deduplication system; its storage evaluation concerns ingestion and columnar
persistence. Parquet groups records into files or chunks suitable for analytical access. Chunk size and writer
behavior can influence file count, metadata overhead, and the time records wait before persistence.
Useful measurements include target feed rate versus actual generator rate, processing throughput,
persistence throughput, queue depth over time, buffer utilization, chunk count, file count, total persisted
bytes, rejected records, and measured write latency. Storage bytes and throughput should be reported for
the exact workload and machine. Do not present theoretical capacity or unmeasured speedups as
benchmark results.

8. Risks and Mitigations
The primary project risks are queue pressure being misreported, differences between live and historical
metrics, incomplete cancellation on Stop, and inconsistencies between persisted files and metadata. These
risks can be reduced through focused tests and by treating backend events and persistence confirmations
as the source of truth.
Another risk is overclaiming production readiness. A local single-process pipeline does not demonstrate
horizontal scaling, durable message replay, replicated storage, or recovery from machine failure. Such
capabilities should be listed as future extensions unless implemented and tested.

9. Acceptance Criteria and Evaluation Plan
Acceptance criteria should be verified against the actual repository and recorded test evidence. The
recommended criteria are: (1) all pipeline stages appear in the correct order and their connections represent
the real data path; (2) preset controls configure real supported parameters; (3) live node values and charts
use consistent backend metrics; (4) target feed rate is distinct from actual throughput; (5) queue depth and
backpressure reflect the real queue; (6) accepted/rejected and persisted counts reconcile with engine
semantics; (7) Stop terminates the active run cleanly; (8) persisted Parquet files can be inspected after a
run; and (9) stored data remains available after a service restart when persistent volumes are configured.

10. Limitations and Recommendation
FlowStore is suitable as a bounded academic virtual lab for explaining time-series ingestion and storage
behavior. It can help demonstrate queueing, validation, partition buffering, chunk formation, and Parquet
persistence. Its results are specific to the implementation, configured workload, and host environment.
Before presenting quantitative conclusions, run each scenario and capture its actual configuration and
outputs. If the project is extended, useful next steps include richer failure injection, stronger recovery and
reconciliation tests, cloud object storage, a durable broker, distributed workers, and additional monitoring.
These are future possibilities and should not be described as existing features without evidence.
